paper_title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID.

sections.content: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve onpolicy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID. 1. Introduction Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can produce inaccurate responses when they under-attend to visual inputs or focus on irrelevant image regions [14, 30]. To improve visual understanding, prior work has strength- *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. Figure 1. Visual values improve predictions more than attention maps. These methods share common focus: 1 they shape the attention weights, denoted as [M], over visual tokens which can be visualized as spatial attention map. However, attention weights are only one half of the mechanism. As shown in Figure 1, panel A, while [M] determines where to attend, the visual value representations, denoted as [V], determine what information is retrieved: the attention readout is the [M]-weighted aggregation of [V] [20]. Existing guidance approaches regulate [M] while leaving [V] unexamined. Given that refining [M] yields only limited gains in grounding accuracy, this raises question: Is visual grounding limited by where the model looks, or by what it retrieves? Answering this question requires disentangling spatial attention patterns from the visual information available at the attended locations. Paired non-contrast and contrastenhanced medical images provide natural testbed for this purpose: they offer anatomically corresponding views while differing in the visual cues revealed by contrast enhancement [13, 47]. Leveraging this property, we construct paired medical VQA diagnostic dataset spanning three anatomical sites and two imaging modalities, where registered image pairs allow the same patient and question to be examined under different visual evidence conditions. Across these paired views, we find that the same model can answer incorrectly from non-contrast image yet correctly from its enhanced counterpart, despite exhibiting similar spatial attention distributions, as shown in Figure 1, panel B. This discrepancy suggests that where the model attends alone cannot fully explain its grounding behavior, motivating us to examine what visual information is retrieved at the attended locations and to leverage the enhanced view as source of privileged visual supervision. Leveraging the spatial correspondence between paired scans, we disentangle [M] and [V] through bidirectional substitution between NC and CE views, with the CE-to-NC direction shown in Figure 1, panel C. Across multiple benchmarks, replacing [V] produces larger changes in model predictions than [M], with directionally consistent effects: enhanced values increase support for the correct answer in the non-contrast branch, while non-contrast values reduce it in the enhanced branch. These controlled interventions indicate that the performance gap between the two views is driven primarily by differences in the visual information carried by [V], rather than by differences in spatical allocation encoded by [M]. In other words, what the model retrieves can matter more than where it attends. Motivated by these findings, we investigate how enhanced visual values can guide knowledge transfer from contrast-enhanced teacher to non-contrast student. While an enhanced-image teacher can provide richer supervision, privileged information does not necessarily translate into effective student supervision, as shown in prior work on In our setting, this motivates exthinking models [17]. amining whether the teachers corrections align with the students response to answer-relevant visual evidence. To allow reasonable [V]-enhanced distillation, we build on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) [57] and propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation). We introduce an auxiliary branch that shares the students non-contrast input and generated answer prefix, while incorporating paired enhanced visual values [V] into the visual readout at attended image locations. The resulting prediction shift captures the students response to enhanced visual evidence and serves as reference direction for the teachers correction. We project the enhanced-image teachers correction onto this direction and retain the positively aligned component as the principal distillation target. At inference, only the non-contrast student is required. Experiments on diverse VQA datasets show that VIVID consistently outperforms off-the-shelf MLLMs and on-policy distillation baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. Revealing what models retrieve beyond where they attend. We establish the first paired medical VQA setting with registered NC and CE scans across three anatomical sites and two imaging modalities. Controlled interventions show that visual values [V] have substantially greater influence on predictions than attention weights [M]., revealing retrieved visual content as critical factor beyond spatial attention patterns. 2. Visual value-guided distillation for non-contrast inference. We propose VIVID, which uses enhanced visual values to better identify relevant teacher corrections and guide knowledge transfer from contrast-enhanced to non-contrast images, while requiring only non-contrast images at inference. 3. Effective and generalizable medical VQA. Extensive experiments across anatomical sites, imaging modalities, and MLLMs architectures demonstrate consistent improvements over existing off-the-shelf MLLMs and onpolicy distillation approaches, together with strong zeroshot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. 2. Related Work 2.1. Attention and Visual Information in MLLMs major line of work improves visual understanding in MLLMs by directing attention toward relevant image regions. PAI amplifies image-token attention with contrastive logit correction [30], while DAMRO suppresses high-attention background outliers [14]. In medical VQA, Localize-before-Answer localizes pathological regions to guide answer generation [36]. These approaches emphasize where models attend, leaving the answer-relevant content retrieved at those locations less directly examined. Earlier Transformer analyses also demonstrate that attention 2 weights alone do not characterize token contributions, highlighting the role of transformed value-vector norms [20]. We examine this distinction through paired NCCE medical images with corresponding anatomy but different diagnostic cues. Despite similar spatial attention patterns, models can produce different answers across views; controlled interventions further reveal that visual values transfer the CE answer advantage more effectively than attention weights. This finding motivates using enhanced visual values to guide learning from non-contrast images. 2.2. Distillation with Privileged Visual Information Contrast administration adds cost and risks adverse reactions [21], motivating knowledge transfer from enhanced to non-contrast images. Prior work focuses on segmentation: HAD-Net distills full-sequence MRI knowledge into student without post-contrast inputs [49], while EGTA-KD transfers enhanced-image knowledge to non-contrast tumor segmentation [56]. Such transfer remains less explored in generative medical VQA. On-policy distillation aligns teacher and student predictions along student-generated sequences [1]. Vision-OPD transfers crop-conditioned perception to full-image student [54]. VA-OPD uses original/degraded-image comparisons to reweight rollouts and balance token groups [29], while Med-OPD uses answer-aware hints to emphasize medically relevant tokens and trajectories [41]. While these approaches improve distillation by adjusting the importance of supervision based on visual dependence or task-relevant evidence, they do not explicitly assess whether teacher corrections align with the students response to privileged visual information. In contrast, VIVID intervenes on visual values using paired CE images to obtain an evidence-induced prediction direction, then retains the positively aligned component of the teachers correction to construct refined distillation targets. 3. Diagnostic Analysis of Visual Understanding To examine whether visual understanding is limited by where the model information it exlooks or by what tracts, we first introduce paired non-contrast and contrastenhanced medical VQA dataset (Sec. 3.1). We then analyze attention patterns and perform controlled attention map and value interventions to assess their respective roles in answer prediction (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3). 3.1. Paired Diagnostic Dataset Construction We construct paired medical VQA dataset covering liver CT, brain MRI, and breast MRI. Data Sources. For liver CT, we use MCT-LTDiag [51] for training and internal evaluation and TriALS [10] for external evaluation. For brain MRI, we train and internally evaluate on cohorts including UPENN-GBM [4] and UCSF-PDGM [5] and other four datasets, with TCGAGBM [45] and TCGA-LGG [39] held out for external evaluation. For breast MRI, we use Duke [44], I-SPY1 [33], and I-SPY2 [25] for training and internal evaluation and NACT [34] for external evaluation. All splits are patientdisjoint. Detailed data sources, statistics, construction procedures, and ethics considerations are provided in Appendices A.1, A.2. Task design. We define three clinically motivated tasks: lesion identification, lesion characterization, and multi-region localization, covering both global and local visual discrimination. We construct QA and supporting evidence at the NCCE pair level: questions and reference answers are derived from segmentation annotations, with the same question, options, and answer assigned to both views of each pair. Concise supporting evidence is generated jointly from the paired views, yielding responses in the Evidence: ... format. Samples undergo clinical ... quality review (see below). Detailed construction process is provided in Appendices A.3 and A.4. Clinial quality assurance. We conduct radiologist-led review before and after full-scale data generation. During the pilot stage, radiologist evaluates generated evidence for spatial consistency and factual accuracy with answer support using two five-point Likert scales. The findings guide revisions to the generation instructions to reduce unsupported inferences and preserve region-specific descriptions. After full-scale generation, the same radiologist reviews 20% sample using the same criteria, obtaining mean scores of 4.6/5.0 and 4.5/5.0, respectively. Detailed procedures and dataset cases are provided in Appendices A.5 and A.6. Answer: 3.2. What Matters to Answering Quality Given frozen models, our analysis focuses on attention to image tokens within the MLLMs decoder during answer generation. At each prediction position, textual query [Q] attends to image-token keys [K], producing spatial attention weights [M]. These weights aggregate the corresponding visual values [V] to form the visual contribution to the attention readout before the output projection. Finding 1: Spatial attention alone does not explain contrasting predictions. We analyze attention maps in MLLMs on paired samples where the NC branch answers incorrectly while the CE branch answers correctly, with each branch generating independently. Despite the difference in prediction correctness, their spatial attention patterns remain remarkably similar. Qualitatively, Fig. 2 shows closely matched attention maps across liver CT, brain MRI, and breast MRI examples. Quantitatively, on liver CT, the fraction of attention assigned to image tokens follows nearly identical layerwise trends between NC and CE inputs in both Qwen3-VL 3 Figure 2. We exchange either [M] or [V] between paired branches while keeping the other component unchanged, and measure changes in correct-answer probability PGT and answer accuracy Acc. We report all-layer results on liver CT here. Analyses of other subsets defined by answer correctness, single-layer interventions, and results for brain and breast MRI are provided in Appendix B.2. Finding 2: Predictions are substantially more sensitive to [V] than to [M]. Table 1 shows clear asymmetry between [M] and [V]. Transferring CE values to the NC branch produces substantially larger gains than transferring CE attention weights, while transferring NC values to the CE branch causes substantially larger degradation. This pattern holds for both Qwen3-VL and MedGemma and across both evaluation protocols. The bidirectional effects indicate that [V] carries much of the answer-relevant difference between paired views that is not captured by their spatial attention patterns. We further conduct stress test to prove that the advantage of CE values does not merely depend on being combined with well-formed NC attention map. After transferring CE values to the NC branch, we progressively perturb its image-attention weights with Gaussian noise while preserving nonnegativity and total image-attention mass. Even under attention weight perturbations, CE values retain gains over the original NC prediction and remain competitive with, or stronger than, transferring CE attention weight alone  (Table 2)  . Although performance decreases as attention becomes noisier, this stress test shows that informative values remain beneficial even when spatial attention becomes less reliable. Thus, attention facilitates the use of visual values, but does not by itself account for their predictive advantage. Finally, we test the robustness of our findings across different basem models. We separately fine-tune NC and CE Qwen3-VL-4B models from the same initialization under identical training configurations. Method Building on our finding that visual values capture answerrelevant differences beyond spatial attention, we revisit how knowledge is distilled from contrast-enhanced teacher to non-contrast student. Existing distillation methods transfer the teachers prediction-level corrections without explicitly accounting for whether these corrections align with the enhanced visual evidence that benefits the student [57]. We therefore extend on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) with Visual Value Intervention Distillation (VIVID), using enhanced visual values to refine targets construction. As illustrated in Figure 4, an auxiliary branch injects paired CE visual values into the NC student along its onpolicy trajectories, as described in Sec. 4.1. The resulting prediction shift captures the students response to enhanced visual evidence and serves as reference direction for refining the target. We retain the positively aligned component of the teachers correction as the distillation signal, thereby using visual values to guide what is distilled rather than distilling them directly, as described in Sec. 4.2. Analysis of Distributions and Visual Values We compare SFT, OPSD, and our method on the liver CT dataset using Qwen3-VL-2B and 4B, examining both predictive distributions and internal visual representations. Task-critical probability allocation. We define margin selectivity (MS) as the difference in average token margin between medical-judgment spans and the remaining evidence tokens, where token margin is the top-1top-2 probability gap. We additionally measure correct-option NLL over the full evaluation set. On questions answered incorrectly by all three models, we report the mean probability assigned to the correct option (P err GT). Our method achieves the best results on all three metrics at both scales  (Table 7)  . These results reveal more selective confidence at task-critical positions alongside stronger support for correct answers, including those that remain unselected. Visual representation changes. We assess alignment with the frozen SFT models enhanced-image visual values using cosine similarity and relative ℓ2 distance over foreground visual values and task-critical readouts . For the attention readout comparison, we apply identical SFT-NC attention weights to all branches. Relative Figure 5. Visual representation improvement relative to OPSD on liver CT dataset. Blue and purple denote Qwen3-VL-2B and 4B. Percentage changes relative to OPSD are grouped by decoder depth: (ad) increased cosine similarity and reduced ℓ2 distance to the enhanced-image reference for visual values and fixed-attention readouts; (e) increased top-ten explained variance; (f) reduced effective rank. Reductions are plotted as positive values. to OPSD, our method improves both alignment measures across all three depth groups, with larger changes generally beyond the early layers (Fig. 5ad). Visual values also exhibit greater top-ten explained variance and lower effective rank, indicating more concentrated spectrum (Fig. 5e,f). Thus, distribution-level distillation is accompanied by closer alignment with enhanced visual representations and more compact spectral structure, without explicit feature-alignment or spectral regularization. Additional analyzes, case studies, and evaluation of generated evidence are provided in Appendices C.4 and C.5. 6. Conclusion We revisit visual understanding in MLLMs beyond spatial attention maps. Using paired NC and CE images, we show that similar attention patterns can lead to different predictions, while controlled interventions reveal that visual values exert greater influence on answer correctness than attention weights. Accordingly, VIVID uses the students response to enhanced visual values to refine teacher supervision for on-policy distillation. Experiments show consistent gains across anatomical sites, modalities, and model architectures. Our findings stress not only where MLLMs attend, but also what information they retrieve, offering perspective on visual understanding and knowledge transfer. 7. sections.content: Lesion-guided slice sampling. For each patient, we select 36 representative lesion-positive slices, prioritizing substantial lesion coverage and diversity in the available lesion-attribute categories. We additionally sample up to two negative slices that contain sufficient anatomical tissue but no lesion for hard negative question construction. To limit redundancy among neighboring slices, we enforce dataset-specific minimum separation in slice indices. This separation is progressively relaxed when too few candidates are available; if the desired sample count still cannot be reached, we retain fewer slices. Question types. We construct three question types spanning slice-level assessment and region-level discrimination, motivated by the combination of global assessment and focal examination in radiological interpretation [23]. Lesion identification asks whether target lesion is present within the queried area, which is either the full slice or highlighted region. Lesion characterization assesses whether lesions are solitary or multiple in liver and breast imaging, or the tumoredema composition in brain imaging. Local visual discrimination asks which of three candidate regions 11 contains target lesion, with an additional None of the above option. Questions and reference answers are derived from segmentation annotations. Region-based questions are omitted when valid candidate regions cannot be constructed. Shortcut mitigation. Clinical image interpretation requires distinguishing suspected lesion from an actual finding: region selected for closer inspection does not necessarily contain lesion. Similarly, lesion elsewhere on the slice does not establish lesion presence within the region under assessment. Motivated by these distinctions, we construct region-based questions that require verifying lesion presence within the specified spatial scope. This design also addresses the tendency of medical VQA models to rely on textual associations or irrelevant image regions rather than question-specific visual evidence [36]. Specifically, we include lesion-negative boxes on lesion-positive slices, requiring models to assess the queried region independently of findings elsewhere. Regional negatives also include candidates mined using NC appearance features. Lesion-characterization questions retain an explicit No lesion option, requiring models to establish lesion presence before assessing multiplicity or tumoredema composition. Likewise, local visual discrimination questions may present three lesion-negative regions even when lesion exists elsewhere on the slice, making None of the above the correct answer. These cases are designed to discourage treating highlighted region, lesion-related question, or an abnormal slice as sufficient evidence of positive finding. Table 9. We derive factual constraints from segmentation annotations, including lesion presence, task-specific lesion attributes, and spatial relationships between lesions and candidate regions. For liver CT, we additionally obtain liver-segment masks using TotalSegmentator [50] and assign lesions to anatomical segments based on spatial overlap. Each paired question receives single evidence statement shared across the NC and CE views, followed by the reference answer in the format Evidence: .... Clinical Review and Quality Assurance Evaluation rubric. radiologist assesses the generated evidence along two dimensions using five-point Likert scales: spatial consistency, which measures agreement with anatomical locations and region annotations, and factual accuracy and answer support, which measures whether the evidence is medically accurate and supports the reference answer. Table 9 and Table 10 provide the scoring criteria. Pilot assessment and prompt refinement. Before fullscale generation, we generate 100 samples for each of the three question types in each dataset. The radiologist reviews all pilot samples, assigning mean scores of 4.3/5.0 for spatial consistency and 4.1/5.0 for factual accuracy and answer support. The primary issue is unsupported inference by the evidence-generating LLM, particularly descriptions of lesion characteristics not established by the supplied information. Based on this review, we revise the generation instructions to constrain evidence to the supplied facts, reference answers, and images, as is provided in Fig. 6. The revised instructions explicitly prohibit unsupported findings and require general descriptions when specific visual characteristics are uncertain. They also enforce the scope of the queried region, preventing lesion absence within marked region from being generalized to the entire image. Post-generation quality assessment. Following full-scale generation with the revised instructions, the same radiologist reviews 20% sample of the generated dataset using the same rubric. Aggregate accuracy may obscure differences across question categories, making it important to examine whether performance gains are concentrated in particular tasks.
